newsitem.title: GERMANY: German universities must reform to win foreigners.
newsitem.headline: German universities must reform to win foreigners.

text.p: German universities must be made more attractive for foreign students, who are flocking instead to institutions mainly in the English-speaking world, a leading academic body said on Tuesday.

"The number of foreign students coming to Germany is really too small, whereas Britain, the U.S., Japan and Australia are all seeing a rapid climb," Theodor Berchem, president of the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) told a news conference.
Germany is worried that it is missing out on potentially valuable ties with future world economic and political leaders, particularly from the growth powerhouse of Asia.

On paper the share of foreigners at German universities rose to 7.3 percent in 1992, or 123,000, from 5.8 percent in 1975, but the quota has actually dropped to 4.1 percent once 40,000 German-born immigrant students are discounted.
The DAAD blamed underfunding of German higher education and said reform of the old-fashioned system was long overdue.
The DAAD's warnings about the drop in foreign students has prompted government concern.
Education Minister Juergen Ruettgers said in December Germany had to be more competitive in the global education market or suffer the academic and economic consequences.
As a first step Ruettgers introduced 12 trial international study courses to be held in German and a foreign language.

Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said last year practices such as an upper age limit of 30 and a 60,000 marks ($37,810) "deposit" on students from developing countries, which put off many students, needed to be changed.

The DAAD, which supports programmes for Germans studying abroad and promotes study in Germany for foreigners, said it wanted to target students from Asia, eastern Europe and Latin America in particular.

Berchem said the aim was not to poach academics and highly qualified people from other countries. "We do not want a brain drain. We want to train people so they can return to their own countries and use what they have learnt," he said.
Christian Bode, the DAAD's general secretary, said attracting more students would not necessarily cost more money.
"We could be more active on the market for students who are self-funded," Bode said, noting that of 60,000 Japanese students who annually study abroad only 1,200 come to Germany.
The DAAD said it also wanted the German system to move to the Anglo-American standard of a Bachelor's degree followed by a Master's degree.
A first degree, or Bachelor's, from a foreign university is not officially recognised in Germany and students wanting to continue their studies here usually have to start from scratch.
Berchem said German universities also needed to market themselves more aggressively. "It's not enough to be good. We must also say we are good," he said. ($1=1.5867 Mark)
